Article Title: In 2014, Naomi Osaka’s family faced eviction while she was still chasing her tennis breakthrough; a year later, she had earned just $6,290 in six months before becoming a four-time Grand Slam champion
Article Text:
Naomi Osaka’s family faced eviction while she was still chasing her tennis breakthrough(Getty Images)

The family gamble behind the Stanford breakthrough

The Grand Slam years changed the scale

From endorsements to investments and ownership

A new chapter in 2026

Naomi Osaka was 16 when her family received an eviction notice on their Florida condominium. Her professional tennis career was still developing, and her earnings were nowhere near enough to provide financial security. A year later, she had earned just $6,290 during the first six months of 2015, a figure that looks very different against the career she would eventually build.More than a decade later, Osaka has four Grand Slam singles titles, a former world No. 1 ranking and a career that stretches beyond tennis into investments, sports ownership, media and fashion.Osaka’s professional journey began with her father, Leonard François, who coached Naomi and her older sister Mari. François was inspired by Richard Williams and chose to develop his daughters outside the traditional American junior tennis system. The family had moved from Japan to the United States when Naomi was three and eventually settled in Florida.The financial pressure became particularly difficult in 2014. According to details from Ben Rothenberg’s biography of Osaka reported by Tennis.com, the family received an eviction notice on their Pembroke Pines condominium about a month before Naomi entered qualifying at the Bank of the West Classic in Stanford.They were given six weeks to leave, at a time when the sisters’ tennis careers had not produced enough income to cover the family’s expenses.The Stanford tournament soon gave Osaka an opportunity to change that picture. The 16-year-old qualified for the main draw and faced Samantha Stosur, the 2011 US Open champion and a former world No. 4. Osaka defeated Stosur in three sets, earning $10,000 in prize money and attracting greater attention from sponsors.Her finances were still modest after the breakthrough. According to the same biography details, Osaka earned only $6,290 during the first six months of 2015, while Mari earned $2,160 during the same period. Osaka was still climbing the professional rankings, with the Grand Slam titles and commercial success that would eventually transform her career still ahead of her.Osaka’s rise accelerated in 2018 when she won her first WTA title at Indian Wells. Later that year, she reached the US Open final and defeated Serena Williams 6-2, 6-4 to claim her first Grand Slam singles championship.The following January brought another major breakthrough. Osaka defeated Petra Kvitova in the 2019 Australian Open final to win her second consecutive Grand Slam title and became the first Japanese player to reach No. 1 in the WTA rankings. She was 21 years and 104 days old when she reached the top position.Naomi Osaka added another US Open title in 2020 and another Australian Open championship in 2021, taking her Grand Slam total to four. Her success also transformed her commercial profile. Forbes estimated that she earned $37.4 million between June 2019 and June 2020, including $34 million from endorsements and $3.4 million in prize money, making her the highest-paid female athlete on its list for that period.That was a dramatic change from the $6,290 she had earned during the first half of 2015. Osaka had gone from a teenager trying to establish herself on the professional circuit to an athlete whose name carried major commercial value, and she began using that platform to pursue opportunities beyond sponsorships.Osaka’s business career began taking a different shape as she started investing in companies and taking ownership positions. In 2019, she invested in BodyArmor and received an equity stake in the sports drink company. Coca-Cola acquired the remaining 85% of BodyArmor in 2021 in a deal that valued the company at $5.6 billion.She also moved into sports ownership. In 2021, Osaka became an investor in the North Carolina Courage of the National Women’s Soccer League. When the club announced the investment, she spoke about the women who had supported her while she was growing up and connected her decision to opportunities for women in sport.“The women who have invested in me growing up made me who I am today,” Osaka said in the club’s announcement. She also said she wanted to invest in women who could become role models and leaders.Her own ventures added another dimension. Osaka launched KINLÒ in 2021, a skincare and suncare brand developed with melanated skin in mind. In 2022, she and Stuart Duguid launched Hana Kuma, a media company focused on stories and creators from different backgrounds. The company later raised $5 million as it expanded its work across entertainment and culture.Osaka has also invested in other consumer businesses. In 2024, she participated in funding rounds involving companies including Pressed Roots and W, adding more ventures to a portfolio that has continued to grow alongside her tennis career.Osaka’s business interests have continued to expand in 2026, with fashion becoming one of her newest areas of focus. In August, she unveiled a prototype for a luxury leather-goods project with designer Mike Cherman at Uncharted’s Fame to Fortune Summit. Osaka described the project as her “biggest dream” outside tennis while explaining how her success in the sport had created opportunities to invest and work with people who could help develop her ideas.Her professional setup also changed at the beginning of the year. Osaka left Evolve, the sports agency she had co-founded with Duguid, at the end of 2025 and returned to IMG for tennis representation in January 2026.On the court, Osaka remains an active professional in 2026, with the WTA listing four Grand Slam titles and a career-high No. 1 ranking. Her return to major competition has added another chapter to a career that has included a rapid rise, a period away from the tour and a return to professional tennis after becoming a mother.The contrast with her early years is difficult to miss. In 2014, her family was dealing with an eviction notice while Osaka was still searching for her first major breakthrough. In the first six months of 2015, she had earned $6,290. Within a few years, her annual earnings were being measured in tens of millions of dollars, while her career expanded into investments, ownership and businesses of her own.In 2026, Osaka is still competing as a Grand Slam champion, but tennis is now only one part of her professional life. Her investments, sports ownership, media work and luxury fashion project show how the platform created by her tennis career has developed into a much broader business career.
Article Summary: Naomi osaka was 16 when her family received an eviction notice on their florida condominium. Her professional tennis career was still developing, and her earnings were nowhere near enough to provide financial security. A year later, she had earned just $6,290 during the first six months of 2015.

NEW DELHI: Shafali Verma continued her sensational run in T20I cricket in 2026, rewriting another record during India's Asian Games gold-medal clash against Sri Lanka on Tuesday.The India opener became the highest run-scorer in a calendar year in women's T20Is, surpassing South Africa's Laura Wolvaardt . Shafali's 29-ball 48 in the gold-medal match took her tally for the year to 863 runs, moving past Wolvaardt's 824.Shafali's innings at Korogi Sports Park featured three fours and three sixes and came at a strike rate of 165.52. Although she fell short of another half-century, her latest contribution extended a remarkable run in the shortest format.In 24 T20Is in 2026, Shafali has now scored 863 runs at an average of 39.22 and a strike rate of 162.83. Her tally includes one century and seven fifties, with a best score of 100 not out.Wolvaardt, meanwhile, has scored 824 runs in 24 matches this year at an average of 43.36 and a strike rate of 138.72. Her tally includes two centuries and four fifties, with a best of 126 not out.Shafali's record-breaking year has been driven by an extraordinary sequence of performances in knockout matches since the 2025 Women's World Cup final.After scoring 87 against South Africa in the World Cup final, she has maintained her aggressive approach across the Asia Cup and Asian Games. Her scores in her last five T20Is read 64, 68, 40 not out, 100 not out and 48.She scored 64 off 40 balls against Bangladesh in the Asia Cup semifinal before following it with 68 off 39 in the final against Sri Lanka.At the Asian Games, Shafali smashed 40 not out from just 15 balls against Japan in the quarterfinal before producing a spectacular unbeaten 100 off 49 balls against Bangladesh in the semifinal.Her 48 against Sri Lanka in the final completed an extraordinary stretch of six innings in which she has amassed 407 runs at an average of 101.75, including one century and three fifties.Shafali's latest milestone came on the same day she and Smriti Mandhana extended their record as the most prolific partnership in women's T20I cricket.The pair's opening stand of 99 against Sri Lanka took their aggregate partnership tally beyond 4,000 runs. Mandhana and Shafali have now combined for 4,080 runs in 107 matches at an average of 39.23, including six century partnerships and 26 fifty-plus stands.The UAE pair of Esha Oza and Theertha Satish are second on the list with 2,949 partnership runs, followed by Australia's Alyssa Healy and Beth Mooney with 2,720.
Article Summary: Shafali verma becomes highest run-scorer in a calendar year in women's t20is. India opener surpasses south africa's laura wolvaardt. Shafali's 29-ball 48 in the gold-medal match took her tally for the year to 863 runs. Mandhana and shafali have now combined for 4,080 runs in 107 matches at an average of 39.23.

Article Title: Michael Jordan retired 23 years ago, Tiger Woods barely plays, yet they still out-earn even Ronaldo and remain the highest-earning athletes in sports history
Article Text:
Michael Jordan (left). Image via: James Gilbert/ Getty Images, Tiger woods (Right). Image via: Instagram

How Jordan and Woods stayed ahead without having to compete

A Fortune That No Longer Depends on the Scoreboard

The Deal Nike Almost Walked Away From

What the Trophies Actually Bought Them

A List Built on What Happens After the Applause Stops

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Michael Jordan has been away from professional basketball since 2003, while Tiger Woods has spent years appearing only intermittently in competitive golf and has not officially retired. Neither is producing the kind of sporting income associated with the world's biggest active stars, yet both remain above them on the all-time earnings list.Michael Jordan has not stepped onto an NBA court in twenty-three years, and Tiger Woods has spent the better part of the last decade managing injuries rather than chasing majors, and yet neither man has been overtaken at the top of sport's all-time earnings ledger. According to Sportico's latest ranking of career earnings through the end of 2025, adjusted for inflation, Jordan sits first with $4.5 billion, Woods follows at $2.88 billion, and only then does the list arrive at Cristiano Ronaldo, the highest-paid athlete still competing, at $2.52 billion. LeBron James and Lionel Messi round out the top five, both of them still playing at the highest level, both of them still a considerable distance behind two men whose competitive careers effectively ended long ago.What makes this year's numbers worth pausing over is not simply that Jordan remains on top, since he has occupied that position for years, but that the gap separating him from Woods grew rather than shrank, expanding from roughly $850 million a year earlier to about $1.31 billion now, a jump of some $460 million in the space of twelve months. Two athletes who no longer need to compete are, in some sense, still winning.There was a period, decades ago now, when Jordan and Woods earned their fortunes the conventional way, by being unmistakably the best at what they did and letting the money follow the performance. Jordan built his early reputation on championships with the Chicago Bulls, and Woods built his on a run of major titles that reshaped what golf could commercially become, and in both cases the athlete and the business around him grew together during those years.Their playing careers have since slowed dramatically, Jordan's ending outright in 2003 and Woods's fading into sporadic, injury-interrupted appearances rather than a formal retirement, and yet the businesses attached to their names kept expanding well past the point where either man could carry them through performance alone.Jordan's estimated earnings for 2025 alone came to $275 million, a figure that quietly exceeded what Ronaldo made over the same period despite Ronaldo still playing at an elite level for Al-Nassr, and it also came to roughly twice the $137 million earned by Canelo Alvarez, who ranked second among active athletes for the year. None of that money arrived through a late-career contract or a surprise return to competitive basketball. It arrived through a business relationship that Jordan signed into as a twenty-one-year-old rookie, one that has since grown so large that its continued output no longer has anything to do with whether Jordan ever plays basketball again.Nike's original agreement with Jordan, signed in 1984 before he had appeared in a single professional game, was worth $2.5 million over five years and included a base salary of $500,000 annually, roughly three times what other NBA players were getting from shoe companies at the time.Buried inside that contract was a clause allowing Nike to exit the deal entirely if Jordan's shoes failed to generate $4 million in sales, a provision that reveals how uncertain the whole arrangement looked at the outset. Nike was, by most measures, an odd choice for a rising basketball star to align himself with, given that Adidas was generating about fifty per cent more revenue at the time, Reebok was closing in fast enough to overtake Nike by 1987, and Converse already had the league's biggest names, including Magic Johnson, Larry Bird and Julius Erving, wearing its shoes.What separated Jordan's contract from those of his contemporaries was a cut of sales built into the terms, meaning that as the shoes sold, his earnings grew alongside them rather than stopping at a fixed salary. Those shoes went on to generate more than $100 million in their first year alone, and the business built on that foundation has continued compounding for four decades, with the Jordan Brand pulling in $7.3 billion in revenue for the fiscal year ending May 2025, even after a sixteen per cent decline during a turnaround led by Nike's chief executive Elliott Hill.Woods, working in a different sport but along a strikingly similar path, spent twenty-seven years under a Nike deal of his own before the partnership ended in 2024, since which time he has built out sponsorships with Rolex, TaylorMade and Monster Energy, alongside ventures spanning golf technology, entertainment, course design and real estate through companies like TMRW Sports, PopStroke and Full Swing, the last of which was acquired by Versant Media Group for approximately $530 million in a deal completed this past August.Woods's competitive record, set against his financial one, tells an unusual story about where professional golf's money actually sits. He has won 82 PGA Tour events and 15 major championships across his career, yet his tournament prize money adds up to only about $121 million, a modest figure next to the nearly $2 billion Forbes estimates he has earned pretax since turning professional.His last major victory came at the 2019 Masters, an improbable comeback at forty-three years old after an eleven-year gap between titles, and his most recent completed PGA Tour event was the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon, where he missed the cut entirely. He did appear at the TGL Finals in March 2026, representing Jupiter Links GC, only to be involved in a rollover car accident three days later that forced him away from the game once again while he recovers from an Achilles tendon rupture sustained the previous year and a seventh back surgery completed in October 2025.Jordan's situation involves no comparable physical setback, simply the passage of twenty-three years since he last competed professionally, and yet Q Scores data cited by Sportico found his public awareness rating still sits at 78 per cent, the highest of any athlete surveyed, with Woods following at 70 per cent alongside Serena Williams, and Shaquille O'Neal and Tom Brady trailing slightly behind at 75 and 73 per cent respectively. Jordan's likability score came in at 28, the highest recorded among the athletes surveyed, while Woods scored 11, actually below the average for sports personalities generally, a gap that suggests the two men's continued earning power rests on different foundations even as their financial outcomes look remarkably similar.Looking across the full ranking rather than just its top two names, the broader pattern becomes harder to ignore. David Beckham, Roger Federer and Tom Brady each earned more than $50 million in 2025 through commercial arrangements alone, despite none of them currently competing in their sports, and the top 50 athletes collectively have generated approximately $56.2 billion in inflation-adjusted earnings through the end of 2025, spanning ten different sports, with basketball contributing the most names at 13, followed by golf with eight and boxing with seven.Only 18 of the 50 athletes on the list remain actively competing, and 20 have crossed the billion-dollar threshold in career earnings, with the cutoff for inclusion sitting around $595 million, a mark currently held by the retired Formula 1 driver Kimi Räikkönen.Serena Williams remains the only woman to appear anywhere on the list, with approximately $680 million in career earnings, and perhaps most tellingly, not a single athlete under the age of 30 has made the cut at all, a gap that seems likely to close given how dramatically on-field salaries and endorsement markets have grown for the current generation.Ronaldo, James and Messi continue adding to their totals every year they keep playing, chasing performance bonuses and new contracts the way athletes always have, while Jordan and Woods sit above them having already crossed into a different category entirely, one where the money keeps arriving regardless of whether either man ever plays again. Jordan stopped being merely a basketball player a long time ago, and it is that transformation, more than anything he ever did on a court, that keeps his name at the very top of a list built to measure exactly this kind of staying power.
Article Summary: Michael jordan has been away from professional basketball since 2003. Tiger woods has spent years appearing only intermittently in competitive golf. Neither is producing the kind of sporting income associated with the world's biggest active stars. Yet both remain above them on the all-time earnings list.

Article Title: Smriti Mandhana scripts history, becomes first woman to score 11,000 international runs
Article Text:
Smriti Mandhana (Pic credit: BCCI Women)

From Mithali Raj's record to 11,000-run landmark

Mandhana, Shafali extend record partnership

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Smriti Mandhana added another landmark to her extraordinary career on Tuesday, becoming the first woman cricketer to complete 11,000 runs in international cricket during India's Asian Games gold-medal final against Sri Lanka at Korogi Sports Park in Aichi-Nagoya.Mandhana entered the final needing just 13 runs to reach the landmark. She had accumulated 10,987 runs across Tests, ODIs and T20Is, with 788 in Tests, 5,411 in ODIs and 4,788 in T20Is. She wasted little time getting to the historic mark after India opted to bat first.The India vice-captain began with two boundaries in the opening over before launching a six in the third over to complete 11,000 international runs. The milestone added another chapter to a remarkable run of record-breaking performances for the left-hander.Mandhana had only recently taken the record for the most runs in women's international cricket across formats from former India captain Mithali Raj . She overtook Raj's tally of 10,868 runs with a spectacular 124 against Hong Kong in the Women's Asia Cup earlier this month, taking her total to 10,880 at the time.The 30-year-old has continued to rewrite the record books in the shortest format as well. During India's Asian Games semifinal against Bangladesh, Mandhana surpassed New Zealand great Suzie Bates to become the leading run-scorer in women's T20Is.She achieved the T20I milestone during her 37 off 19 balls in India's 114-run win over Bangladesh. At that point, Mandhana moved to 4,788 T20I runs, ahead of Bates' 4,758.Her latest landmark in the Asian Games final came just two weeks after she had established herself as the leading run-scorer in women's international cricket. Her 124 against Hong Kong was also her 18th international century, taking her past Meg Lanning and Laura Wolvaardt for the most hundreds in women's international cricket at the time.Mandhana's rapid accumulation of milestones has made the Asian Games a particularly memorable tournament for her. She also became the first Indian woman to hit 100 sixes in T20Is during the semifinal against Bangladesh.Mandhana also reached her half-century in the gold-medal clash off just 31 balls, continuing her aggressive start alongside Shafali Verma.The pair's latest stand further extended their record as the most prolific partnership in women's T20I cricket. Their aggregate partnership runs moved beyond 4,000, comfortably ahead of the UAE's Esha Oza and Theertha Satish, who are second on the list with 2,949 runs.Their partnership in the final also crossed another significant mark, with Mandhana and Shafali adding 99 runs against Sri Lanka on Tuesday.India entered the final unchanged after beating Japan by eight wickets in the quarterfinal and Bangladesh by 114 runs in the semifinal. Sri Lanka also retained the same XI after overcoming Malaysia and Pakistan to reach the gold-medal match. India's semifinal win was powered by Shafali's unbeaten 100 off 49 balls.The final is a rematch of the 2023 Asian Games gold-medal clash, as well as the Women's Asia Cup final earlier this month, both won by India. India are defending their Asian Games title after winning gold in their only previous appearance in the women's cricket event in 2023.Sri Lanka, meanwhile, are seeking their first Asian Games gold after winning bronze in 2014 and silver in 2022. Mandhana's 11,000-run milestone has added another historic subplot to the gold-medal showdown.
Article Summary: Smriti mandhana becomes the first woman cricketer to complete 11,000 runs in international cricket during india's asian games gold-medal final against sri lanka. The 30-year-old entered the final needing just 13 runs to reach the landmark. She had accumulated 10,987 runs across tests, odis and t20is, with 788 in tests, 5,411 in ois and 4,788 in t20s.

Article Title: Asian Games: Sakshi Chaudhary beats Paris Olympics bronze medallist Aira Villegas to enter pre-quarters
Article Text:
Sakshi Chaudhary (Image credit: X)

Tough challenge awaits Sakshi

Sakshi follows CWG gold with Asian Games win

'I play for my country'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Sakshi keen to learn from CWG experience

Commonwealth Games gold medallist Sakshi Chaudhary made a winning start to her Asian Games campaign by beating Paris Olympics bronze medallist Aira Villegas of the Philippines in the preliminary round on Tuesday.Sakshi won the bout 5-0 by unanimous decision at the Nishio Gymnasium and booked her place in the pre-quarterfinals.The Indian boxer won all three rounds unanimously, with all five judges giving her a 10-9 score in each round. Sakshi looked in control throughout and her accurate punches troubled Villegas.Sakshi will now face a much tougher test in the pre-quarterfinals.The Commonwealth Games gold medallist will take on current 51kg world champion Alua Balkibekova on Thursday.The Indian boxer has already beaten some of the leading names in the sport.She defeated two-time world champion Nikhat Zareen and reigning world champion Minakshi Hooda during the selection trials for the Commonwealth Games 2026.After moving down from 54kg, Sakshi beat Nikhat in the semifinal of the trials before defeating 48kg champion Hooda in the final to earn her place at the Commonwealth Games.Sakshi went on to win gold at the Commonwealth Games 2026.She defeated England's Ruby White 5-0 in the final.After her successful Commonwealth Games campaign, Sakshi turned her attention towards the Asian Games."Winning a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games is a dream come true moment for me. And now my complete focus is on the Asian Games. These are the platforms that I have always aimed at, and I want to give the best of my abilities," Sakshi had said.Sakshi has also spoken about the motivation she gets from representing India.The boxer said playing for her country gives her the strength to keep improving with every bout."I play for my country. This constant thought pumps me up and gives me the strength and courage to do better than the last match I played," she added.Sakshi had also said she would immediately start preparing for the Asian Games after her Commonwealth Games campaign.She wanted to use the lessons from the CWG to improve her performance in Japan."I will begin my training for the Asian Games now. I have learnt a lot from my Commonwealth matches, and I will always cherish this experience," she had added before the Asiad.Sakshi will now look to carry her strong form into Thursday's pre-quarterfinal against Balkibekova.
Article Summary: Sakshi chaudhary beat aira villegas of the philippines 5-0 in the preliminary round of the asian games. The indian boxer won all three rounds unanimously, with all five judges giving her a 10-9 score in each round. Sakshi will now face current 51kg world champion alua balkibekova on thursday.

Article Title: Smriti Mandhana, Richa Ghosh power India to highest-ever Asian Games total in gold-medal match vs Sri Lanka
Article Text:
Team India (Pic credit: BCCI Women)

SCORECARD:

Mandhana lays foundation before Richa's late assault

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Smriti Mandhana 's blistering 79 and Richa Ghosh's explosive unbeaten 49 helped India post a daunting 216/3, their highest-ever total in women's cricket at the Asian Games, against Sri Lanka in the gold-medal match at the Korogi Sports Park on Tuesday.Batting first after Harmanpreet Kaur won the toss, India came out attacking from the outset, with Mandhana setting the tone in the opening over. The left-hander struck two boundaries off Sugandika Kumari before continuing her assault in the third over, smashing two successive sixes off the Sri Lankan bowler.Shafali Verma soon joined the party, and India raced to 40/0 after four overs. The fifth over, bowled by Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu, yielded 19 runs, including three sixes, as the opening pair took India to 59/0. India finished the powerplay at 67/0.Mandhana reached her 37th T20I half-century from 31 balls in the 10th over. The milestone was even more significant as she also became the first woman cricketer to complete 11,000 runs in international cricket.However, India lost Shafali later in the same over. Chamudi Praboda dismissed the opener for a brisk 48 off 29 balls, ending India's 99-run opening partnership.Shafali's innings featured three fours and three sixes.Mandhana continued to anchor India's innings as Harmanpreet joined her in the middle. The pair took India to 123/1 after 13 overs before Kavisha Dilhari ended their 42-run partnership by dismissing Harmanpreet for 19 off 17 balls.Richa then joined Mandhana and immediately maintained the tempo. The pair added 15 runs from Praboda's 16th over, taking India to 157/2.Sri Lanka finally got the prized wicket of Mandhana in the 17th over when Sugandika Kumari dismissed her for 79 off 45 balls. Mandhana's innings included five fours and seven sixes, leaving India at 163/3.There was no let-up in India's scoring after her departure. Richa took charge, smashing 14 runs from Kavya Kavindi's over as India crossed 180.The wicketkeeper-batter saved her most damaging assault for the final over. Taking on Mithali Ayodhya, Richa smashed 17 runs to propel India to 216/3 after 20 overs.Richa remained unbeaten on 49 off just 22 balls, with six fours and three sixes, narrowly missing a half-century but ensuring India finished with a formidable total.For Sri Lanka, Praboda, Dilhari and Kumari claimed one wicket apiece.The 216/3 surpassed India's previous best total in women's cricket at the Asian Games and gave the defending champions a substantial platform as they looked to retain the gold medal.
Article Summary: Mandhana becomes first woman cricketer to complete 11,000 runs in international cricket. Richa remains unbeaten on 49 off just 22 balls, with six fours and three sixes. India post highest-ever total in women's cricket at the asian games.

Article Title: NBA contract update: Toronto Raptors signs 23-year-old 6-foot-3er guard to multi-year deal for $9.4 million
Article Text:
Jaden Bradley gets four-year commitment from Raptors. Image via: Aryanna Frank-Imagn Images

Jaden Bradley lands four-year Raptors deal

Bradley now fights for backup point guard minutes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jaden Bradley just turned a training camp battle into a four-year paycheck. The Toronto Raptors converted the 23-year-old guard's two-way contract into a standard deal worth $9.3 million on Monday, according to Michael Scotto of HoopsHype, with the first season fully guaranteed.Toronto's roster had dropped to 13 players once the long-negotiated Kawhi Leonard trade finally cleared, sending Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick out west. Someone had to fill that open standard spot, and Bradley made the case himself.Jaden Bradley arrived in Toronto as the 50th pick of the 2026 draft, a slot usually reserved for camp fodder, not four-year commitments. He signed a two-way deal back on July 6 and spent the summer trying to make himself impossible to cut loose.He didn't dominate Summer League so much as show some unforgettable moments. Across five games, the Rochester, New York native averaged 6.4 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.2 assists in just over 20 minutes a night, topping out at 15 points and five boards in a July 13 win over Indiana. Scotto's report on the new deal noted that "this first year of the deal is guaranteed," a detail that matters for a player who came in as one of the draft's final names.Bradley spent his final three college seasons at Arizona after starting his career at Alabama, where he made the All-SEC freshman team. By his senior year with the Wildcats, he was Big 12 Player of the Year, averaging 13.3 points, 4.4 assists, 3.4 rebounds and 1.4 steals while shooting 39.4 percent from three. He picked up Big 12 Tournament MVP and consensus Third Team All-American honors along the way and helped drag Arizona to its first Final Four in 25 years.None of that guarantees playing time in Toronto. Bradley will spend training camp, which opens September 29 in Quebec City, competing for backup point guard reps behind Immanuel Quickley, with fellow Big 12 products Jamal Shead and Ja'Kobe Walter already in that mix. It's a crowded lane for a player who was a fringe draft name three months ago.Toronto didn't leave its two-way roster thin in the process. The team filled Bradley's old two-way slot with former Gonzaga guard Malachi Smith, keeping that development pipeline active even as Bradley graduates to the standard roster.For now, the deal looks like an investment rather than a promise for playing minutes. The Raptors are betting that the ball-handling, defense, and playmaking instincts that carried Arizona to a Final Four run translate better once an NBA season actually starts. Bradley gets four years and a guaranteed first season to prove it.
Article Summary: Jaden bradley signed a two-way deal with the toronto raptors back on july 6. The 23-year-old guard now has a four-year contract worth $9.3 million, with the first season fully guaranteed. Bradley will compete for backup point guard minutes in training camp.

Article Title: Chess Olympiad Round 6: How Nihal Sarin blundered his queen, and India suffered heartbreaking loss to Uzbekistan
Article Text:
Nihal Sarin at Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza from FIDE)

India's women back to winning ways

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: On Monday, India's open team was paired against hot favourites and tournament hosts Uzbekistan in Round 6 of the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand.The anticipation around this fixture had been building since before the tournament began, perhaps because these two nations have won the last two Olympiads between them, or because Dommaraju Gukesh will face Javokhir Sindarov for the World Championship later this year, or simply because these are, right now, two of the most potent chess nations on the planet.India had arrived at the board sitting in the leading group after five rounds, level with Uzbekistan and Germany at the top of the standings, which only added to the stakes. Hence, captain Srinath Narayanan put the strongest line-up forward, with Praggnanandhaa on Board 1, Arjun Erigaisi on 2, Nihal Sarin on 3, and Gukesh on 4.Consequently, Vidit Gujrathi had a rest day, thanks to which he was momentarily part of the ChessBase India commentary team at the venue.His eyes lit up when Nodirbek Yakubboev, playing White, pushed 35.f4 against Nihal. With every other board on the day ending in or heading towards a draw, this was the one game left with a winner in it.Nihal replied 35...e3, and Vidit's eyes only became brighter. Yakubboev's 36.fxg5+ put India in a genuinely promising position.But then what followed was a sequence no Indian fan would have wanted to see — 36...Kxg5 37.g3 Nf5.Vidit felt Nihal, sensing a clear advantage, got swept up in the moment and pushed a little too hard. Soon after, his queen was captured (40.Qxc7), and the entire commentary panel, Vidit included, could only put their hands on their heads.The disappointment was more palpable because Nihal still had plenty of time left on the clock. This wasn't a case of time pressure forcing a mistake, just a hanging piece missed in the heat of a winning position. But that is what it was.Amid all that activity, Nihal's queen was left completely undefended on c7. Yakubboev's 40.Qxc7 simply took it for free.From a position where Black had real winning chances just a few moves earlier, the game swung entirely in White's favour, and Yakubboev converted the resulting material advantage into a full point without much further resistance.It proved decisive. With Praggnanandhaa, Erigaisi and Gukesh all drawing their games on the other three boards, Nihal's loss was the difference. Uzbekistan won the match 2.5-1.5, handing India their first team defeat of the tournament in the open section.India's women, by contrast, had a comfortable day at the office after a Round 5 defeat to Poland, beating the United States 3-1 on Monday.Koneru Humpy and Divya Deshmukh both drew their games against higher-pedigree opposition in Carissa Yip and Alice Lee, but the difference came further down the order, with Vantika Agrawal beating the experienced Irina Krush, and Savitha Shri getting the better of Rose Atwell.Tuesday is the tournament's only scheduled rest day, a timely break for India's open side after a result that will sting more for how close it came to going the other way than for the actual damage on the scoreboard.Play resumes on Wednesday with Round 7, when India's open team takes on England, and the women's team faces Germany.
Article Summary: India's open team was paired against hot favourites and tournament hosts uzbekistan in round 6 of the 46th chess olympiad in samarkand. Vidit gujrathi had a rest day, thanks to which he was momentarily part of the chessbase india commentary team. Uzbekistan won the match 2.5-1.5, handing india their first team defeat of the tournament in the open section.

Article Title: ‘Virat Kohli inspires me’: Himanshu Dhillon’s dream Asian Games debut with two silvers
Article Text:
India's Rudrankksh Patil, left, wins bronze medal and Himanshu Dhillon wins Silver medal (PTI Photo)

From wrestling to shooting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Himanshu Dhillon is a diehard Sunny Deol fan. His father, Shamsher Dhillon, has a doctorate in agriculture. The shooter’s motivational mantra, then, paraphrases a famous dialogue of his idol, his father’s profession and the farming he tried during the pandemic.“Yeh kisaan ka haath hai. Yeh lohe ko pighla kar uska aakaar badal deta hai (This is the hand of a farmer. He melts iron and shapes it).”On Monday, Dhillon didn’t melt metal; instead, he shot two of them, both silver, in the 10m air rifle at the Aichi Prefecture Shooting Range.First, the Asian Games debutant teamed up with Rudrankksh Patil and Parth Mane to clinch the men’s team silver. He returned later in the afternoon and, in a pulsating display of composure, concentration and precision, finished second (252.4) in the individual event, opening his individual tally at the senior international level.Patil, who at one stage held a 1.5-point lead, faltered and settled for bronze (230.9).It took a Games record by the reigning Olympic and Asian Games champion Lihao Sheng (254.2) to climb to the top of the podium. The Chinese shooter bettered his mark of 253.3 from the previous Games.Dhillon’s father sends him motivational messages daily. On the day, first came his 21st birthday wishes, followed by a message which read: “Whatever happens, you need to add a medal for India.The colour of the medal depends on you.”The message, in his native tongue, seemed to strike a chord. While Patil hit the front, Sheng and Dhillon played catch-up. A 10.2 and 9.7 relegated Patil. Dhillon was also pegged back by a 9.8, which gave the Chinese the unassailable lead, but his three 10.9s did the trick.It was a contest of fine margins, with four 10.9s in an elimination series and three shoot-offs deciding positions.Dhillon’s journey is only beginning, but the junior World Cup gold medallist already has an eye on the legacy he would like. In shooting, he idolises Abhinav Bindra . His sporting hero, though, is Virat Kohli “I’m very inspired by Virat Kohli,” he said.As he walked away with two silver medals around his neck, the significance of the day was not lost on him.“This is the best birthday gift I could have given myself,” he said.But he did not begin as a shooter. Inspired by his uncle Hardeep Singh Dhillon, who represented India in Greco-Roman wrestling at the 2016 Rio Olympics, his father enrolled him in an akhada. It took just two weeks to realise wrestling was not for him.“I found wrestling a bit hard, so I later opted for shooting while studying in a Gurukul in Kudri,” he said with a laugh.Once he found his calling at the range, his family backed him despite financial constraints.“My parents left our village for me. It’s their sacrifices that have got me here,” he said.
Article Summary: Himanshu dhillon won two silver medals in the 10m air rifle at the aichi prefecture shooting range. He teamed up with rudrankksh patil and parth mane to clinch the men’s team silver. He returned later in the afternoon and, in a pulsating display of composure, concentration and precision, finished second in the individual event.

Article Title: “Three-against-one situation”: El Rubius opens up on being “targeted” in MrBeast’s viral $1M challenge
Article Text:
El Rubius reacted honestly after his elimination from MrBeast’s $1 million challenge, calling it “unfair” and claiming he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings. His response felt real and balanced, especially after MrBeast’s team later sent him a cake, softening the moment.

El Rubius reflects on a tough and “unfair” exit

El Rubius did not just walk away from MrBeast’s $1 million streamer challenge. He opened up. Soon after his elimination, the Spanish creator shared a raw reaction with fans, giving them a closer look at what the experience felt like from inside the game. It was not polished or carefully framed. It felt real, and that is exactly why it caught attention so quickly.The clip and his response have since fueled conversations across the streaming space. Some viewers believe intense competitions like this naturally lead to uneven situations. Others feel Rubius may have had a point about being singled out. Either way, his words have added a human layer to a challenge that many only saw as entertainment.Speaking through an Instagram Story, Rubius did not hide his frustration, but he also made sure to thank his supporters. He said, "Guys, I just got knocked out of the game. It was a bit of an unfair elimination, but hey, at least I managed to walk away with $50,000 for you all, which I’ve already distributed. It went to the mods, the subs, and the non-subs alike."He further added, "I’m happy, of course, though admittedly, it was incredibly tough.I wasn't really a fan of the challenge itself, either. But then again... it was basically a three-against-one situation the entire time. I mean, they were targeting me specifically the whole way through. I kept trying to go after RaKai, but, well, he actually just got eliminated in the end. So, at least justice was served for Abraham. Abraham, if you’re watching this, we were all rooting for you, and standing right there with you."His message carried mixed emotions. There was disappointment, yes, but also pride in how he handled things. Giving away his $50,000 winnings to his community stood out as a gesture that meant more than the result itself.He continued with another honest note, saying, "And in the end, karma finally caught up with that little punk. Sorry, I’m being a bit toxic right now, but let's just hope the MrBeast team doesn't see this! Guys, thank you all so much. Seriously, thank you for all the support and for just being there."He added, "Every time I asked for something in the chat or whatever it was, you guys were right there. You’re incredible. I’m a little disappointed in myself, personally, mostly for not performing better, but hey, I gave it my all, and we still walked away with $50,000, so we’ve got to look on the bright side. All right, guys, big hugs to all my brothers out there!"Interestingly, the story did not end with frustration. Later that day, Rubius revealed that MrBeast’s team had sent him a cake after his exit. It was a small gesture, but it shifted the mood. It showed that even in a high-pressure challenge, there is still room for respect.In the end, Rubius’ reaction felt honest and grounded. That is what stayed with people.
Article Summary: El rubius was eliminated from mrbeast's $1 million challenge. He called it "unfair" and said he was targeted in a three-against-one situation. Despite his frustration, he thanked fans and gave away his $50,000 winnings.

Article Title: In 2007, Scottish cyclist Mark Beaumont left Paris to race around Earth; 194 days and 17 hours later, crashes, theft and exhaustion had not stopped him
Article Text:
Scottish adventurer Mark Beaumont is pictured during his long-distance cycling career and carrying the Olympic torch during the London Olympics torch relay. Beaumont carried the flame across the Forth Road Bridge in Scotland. Credits - Wikipedia

A path through hardship

Mark Beaumont cycles alongside a local rider and a donkey-drawn cart in eastern Pakistan during his 2007–08 record-setting journey around the world by bicycle. Credits - Wikipedia

Rewriting the record

Long before ultra-endurance sport became a global spectacle, crossing the world on two wheels was the domain of the odd and the dreamer. Record keepers had been tracking efforts at this achievement for decades, and the bar kept moving as riders pushed further into the unknown with little more than paper maps, panniers and persistence. A young man from rural Fife, a man who had spent his childhood cycling throughout Scotland for enjoyment, stepped into that bloodline in the summer of 2007. What came next would see him become one of the defining figures in endurance riding and rewrite what people thought was physically feasible on a bicycle.On 5 August 2007, Mark Beaumont left the Arc de Triomphe in Paris on a laden touring bike with an objective that appeared almost reckless for someone who had never attempted anything on this scale before. He planned to ride about 100 miles a day, alone and unsupported, until he had travelled round the globe and got back to where he started. His bicycle, a Koga Miyata with a Rohloff internal gear hub, was loaded with around 30 kilogrammes of tools, spare parts and video equipment, since he was chronicling the voyage himself for what would become a BAFTA nominated BBC film. Cycling UK , the membership club that has long backed British riders on just this sort of personal endeavour, later published his own report of how three years of planning went into that single departure from Paris.Beaumont’s journey carried him east via Europe and Russia, through Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, across Southeast Asia and Australia, and then across North America before one more trans-Atlantic trip back to France. It was a tough trail, and preparation wouldn’t make it easier. In Lafayette, Louisiana, he was hit by a car and robbed later that same day, an experience that would have killed most people’s endeavours on the spot. Elsewhere he fought illness and the sort of physical disintegration that comes from sixteen or more hours a day in the saddle for months on end without rest. He’d also meant to be a vegetarian but had little choice but to give that up during the ride simply to keep enough calories going in to survive the daily mileage.It’s not only the distance but also the isolation that makes the achievement exceptional. Throughout the ride, Beaumont had no support car, no mechanic and no chef. If his gear broke or his body let him down, he had to tackle the problem himself, often in isolated parts of Pakistan, Iran or the Australian outback where help was hours or days away. He used paper maps in an age when smartphone navigation didn’t even exist for bikes and had his mother back home assist him in plotting alternative routes if roads were blocked.On 15 February 2008, Beaumont cycled back past the Arc de Triomphe, having completed almost 18,000 miles in 194 days and 17 hours. That broke the previous world record by 81 days, a margin so vast that even veteran endurance athletes who had thought the mark would stand for years were startled. His accomplishment was officially validated, and the lineage of riders who chased and ultimately beat his time is still recorded on the official Guinness World Records page for the quickest circumnavigation by bicycle. Other cyclists would eventually beat Beaumont's own record, such as Vin Cox in 2010, before Beaumont himself recaptured the supported version of the championship in 2017 with a specially organised support squad, further lowering his own original time.But it is the 2007 solo ride that attracted public attention, because he did it without a safety net. Beaumont then returned to his old university, the University of St Andrews , to speak to students about the trip. He didn't frame it as some prank, but as proof that ordinary preparedness, stubbornness and a tolerance for discomfort might take a person further than nearly anyone expected. The ride raised £18,000 for charity and he utilised the platform it established to launch a series of additional expeditions including the length of the Americas trip from Alaska to Argentina and a solo unsupported crossing from Cairo to Cape Town.Nearly two decades later, Beaumont's original circumnavigation is still cited as a moment when unsupported round-the-world cycling moved from an oddity to a recognised branch of endurance sport, inspiring later solo riders like Jenny Graham and a wave of amateur cyclists who attempt similar routes every year. It’s not just the miles that keep the story alive, but what it said about the extremes individuals will reach when curiosity and discipline collide.
Article Summary: Mark beaumont left the arc de triomphe in paris on a laden touring bike in august 2007. He planned to ride about 100 miles a day, alone and unsupported, until he had travelled round the globe and got back to where he started. His bicycle, a koga miyata with a rohloff internal gear hub, was loaded with around 30 kilogrammes of tools, spare parts and video equipment.

Article Title: Meet Roger Cettina, 59, the Hall of Fame horse racing fan who turned $2 teenage bets into nearly $500,000 and helped rebuild Belmont Park
Article Text:
Roger Cettina, 59, went from $2 teenage wagers to nearly $500,000 in horseplaying wins before helping rebuild the legendary racetrack. (Photo: Lone Pine Press)

From teenage bets to nearly $500,000 in winnings

Roger Cettina finished runner-up in the National Horseplayers Championship twice, won nearly $500,000 and was inducted into the NHC Hall of Fame. (Photo: Lone Pine Press)

The ‘master’ of horseplaying

From racing fan to Belmont Park builder

After visiting Belmont Park as a teenager, Roger Cettina returned decades later as part of the team rebuilding the iconic Long Island racetrack. (Photo: Lone Pine Press)

A dream job for a lifelong fan

For Roger Cettina, rebuilding Belmont Park was the kind of opportunity that could only come around once in a lifetime.The 59-year-old senior vice president at AECOM Tishman had spent decades as a passionate horse racing fan, making modest $2 and $5 bets as a teenager before becoming a serious competitor in national horseplayer contests. Years later, his love for the sport brought him back to the legendary Long Island racetrack - this time not as a spectator, but as one of the people helping rebuild it.“Our company was lucky enough to get the contract to do this, and it was a once-in-a-lifetime thing,” Cettina told The New York Post ahead of the racetrack’s grand opening.“Like, wow, a horse player like me could actually build the new Belmont Park — someplace that I came so often when I was younger,” he added.Cettina’s fascination with horse racing began while growing up in Tenafly, New Jersey. As a boy, he would spend afternoons at Belmont Park before heading back to New Jersey for night races at the Meadowlands in East Rutherford.His own betting began modestly at 18 and 19, when he would wager just $2 or $5. About 15 years ago, however, he stepped into the world of high-stakes horseplayer competitions, sometimes putting more than $5,000 of his own money into contests.For Cettina, it was never simply about making money. He saw horse racing as an intellectual challenge - something that complemented rather than replaced his construction career.“I enjoyed it. It’s math,” he said. “It’s a puzzle – trying to figure things out, and it’s just something that I totally got into.”That approach paid off spectacularly.In 2013, Cettina finished second in the National Horseplayers Championship, winning $200,000 after competing against hundreds of entries over three days.“There are eight or 900 entries that you’re playing against, and it’s over three days,” he explained.“You bet basically to win and place on 15 races a day from all over the country, and whoever has the highest cumulative total wins.”Cettina missed out on first place by just $1.20. But the runner-up finish still proved hugely lucrative, and his wife Wendy certainly appreciated the prize money, particularly after he bought her a new Lexus.Two years later, Cettina did it again.He finished runner-up in the 2015 championship, collecting another $230,000.“I cashed almost a half a million dollars between the two – and I’ve definitely not put that much money into it,” he said.Cettina also co-owns two horses and credits luck as one ingredient in his success.“You have to be really lucky,” he said.Cettina’s two runner-up finishes made him the only National Horseplayers Championship contestant to finish second more than once.The Daily Racing Form dubbed him “the master” of his craft in 2016. A year later, he was inducted into the NHC Hall of Fame.His results fluctuated in the years that followed, but Cettina estimates that he has made around $300,000 in net profit from horse racing over his lifetime.“Not nearly enough to retire,” he joked. “Not in New York and New Jersey.”So the construction business remained his day job.Cettina worked on major projects including the Goldman Sachs headquarters in Lower Manhattan, renovations to the Javits Center and One and Two Manhattan West near Hudson Yards.But in 2024, an opportunity arrived that combined both of his passions: construction and horse racing.Cettina became part of the team tasked with reconstructing Nassau County’s iconic racing venue from the ground up.There was, however, one major complication. By then, Cettina had moved roughly 75 miles south to Sea Bright on the Jersey Shore.“I went home and talked to my wife about it because obviously I couldn’t commute,” he recalled.Wendy agreed to the unusual arrangement. Cettina began staying during the week in a friend’s basement in West Hempstead and occasionally at another friend’s home in the Bronx near the Throgs Neck Bridge.“Then I packed my bags – and here I am,” he said.For the next two years, Cettina spent his weekdays working at Belmont Park before heading back to the Jersey Shore on weekends.Working on the new Belmont Park gave Cettina the rare chance to combine the career he had built with the sport he had loved since childhood.“I don’t know of any other workers that are actually into this like I am,” he said.For someone who once stood at Belmont Park as a teenager placing small bets, the transformation was extraordinary.“It was an unbelievable experience, and the chance for me to build a racetrack was just incredible,” Cettina said.
Article Summary: Roger cettina, 59, went from $2 teenage wagers to nearly $500,000 in horseplaying wins before helping rebuild the legendary racetrack. The senior vice president at aecom tishman made modest $2 and $5 bets as a teenager before becoming a serious competitor in national horseplayer contests.

NEW DELHI: Fireworks were expected when left-handed opener Abhishek Sharma walked out alongside Sanju Samson against Japan at the Sano International Cricket Ground on Tuesday.But Abhishek's stay at the crease lasted just one ball.India captain Shreyas Iyer won the toss and opted to bat in the rain-hit five-over-a-side clash. Samson faced five balls and scored a single before giving the strike to Abhishek.Japan immediately made the breakthrough as Charlie Hara-Hinze dismissed Abhishek for a golden duck.Hara-Hinze bowled one on leg stump and Abhishek crouched low to try and help the ball along. However, he only managed a top edge, with Shoma Sugaya-Slater running back to complete a good catch.Abhishek was dismissed for 0 off 1, leaving India at seven runs with the big wicket of their explosive opener.The dismissal was Abhishek's fifth first-ball duck in T20Is in 2026, putting him level with Rwanda's Kevin Irakoze (2023) and Richard Ngarava (2024) for the most first-ball ducks by a batter in a calendar year in men's T20Is.His five first-ball ducks in T20Is this year have come against New Zealand, USA, Ireland, New Zealand and Japan.Abhishek has also registered 10 ducks in T20 cricket in 2026, the most by a batter in a calendar year. Rashid Khan had nine ducks in 2019, while Shadab Khan also recorded nine in 2024.The India opener is also among the batters with the most ducks in a calendar year in T20Is, with seven such dismissals in 2026.

The 7th PNB MetLife Junior Badminton Championship shattered records with over 8,200 young talent nationwide, earning global recognition and fostering a culture of resilience and determination in aspiring badminton starsIn a spectacular display of badminton prowess and youthful enthusiasm, the 7th edition of the PNB MetLife Junior Badminton Championship (JBC) etched its name in the annals of sporting history. Celebrating a staggering participation of 8257 young champions from across India, the championship not only broke its own record set in 2022 but also clinched the title of the ‘Most kids participating in a Badminton Championship in multiple cities’ as recognised by the World Record Certification Agency (WRCA).The grand finale unfolded at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in New Delhi, where the air was thick with competition, camaraderie, and the unmistakable passion for badminton. The event, graced by chief guests Chirag Shetty and Satwik Rankireddy, Asian Games Gold Medalists and JBC 2023 mentors, was a true celebration of the sport’s rising stars.The 10-city extravaganza, spanning the length and breadth of the country, showcased the unwavering commitment of PNB MetLife in nurturing young talents in the badminton arena. With participants exceeding 8200, it’s evident that the PNB MetLife JBC has become a beacon for aspiring shuttlers, highlighting the deep-seated passion for badminton among the diverse and talented youth of India.Beyond the glitz and glamour of the record-breaking numbers, the championship holds a special place in the hearts of those at the helm. Ashish Kumar Srivastava, MD and CEO of PNB MetLife, expressed pride in not just surpassing their own world record but also in contributing to India’s glory on the international badminton stage. The championship, he emphasized, is not merely a competition but a significant milestone in creating a pan-India badminton ecosystem.This edition of the JBC saw a strategic partnership with world champions Chirag Shetty and Satwiksairaj Rankireddy, who served as mentors for the young talents. Article Title: Marvel's Wolverine hotfix finally dims the scent trails
Article Text:
Insomniac has reduced the opacity of Marvel's Wolverine's Scent Trails and Audio Sense indicators in update 1.001.005, with a full toggle still under consideration.

A full off switch is on the table, but Insomniac has not committed to one

Insomniac Games has rolled out the first fix for the most mocked part of Marvel's Wolverine. Update 1.001.005, released on 18 September, reduces the opacity of the game's Scent Trails and Audio Sense indicators so the glowing paths that steer Logan toward his next objective sit lighter on screen. The studio describes the change as making the visuals "less intense". The same download also clears a set of crashes that a small share of players had been running into since launch.The trails, nicknamed fart trails by players, became the lightning rod for a broader complaint. Critics argued that a linear action game does not need constant signposting, and that the combination of trails, on-screen markers and prompting voice lines left almost nothing in the level for the player to work out.The patch notes say the team is still evaluating ways to improve the Senses systems, including toggleable options in a future update. No date is attached, and no promise has been made that the trails can be turned off completely. A separate UV bug is also queued for a fix, according to community and marketing director James Stevenson, who said ahead of release that the team had been "cooking hard" on feedback.Marvel's Wolverine is a PS5 exclusive and currently sits as the lowest-rated single-player AAA release from a PlayStation first-party studio since Days Gone in 2019. Player scores on PSN and aggregator sites have landed noticeably higher than review scores.For now, the guidance is quieter rather than gone. Whether it disappears entirely is a decision Insomniac has pushed to a later patch.
Article Summary: Insomniac games has rolled out the first fix for the most mocked part of marvel's wolverine. Update 1.001.005 reduces the opacity of the game's scent trails and audio sense indicators so the glowing paths that steer logan toward his next objective sit lighter on screen.

Article Title: Nike Alphafly 4 launched with lighter ZoomX LT foam and 10% more energy return
Article Text:
Nike Alphafly 4 are 5% lighter than Alphafly 3

Two foams now sandwich the plate

The upper is designed for tired feet

Nike has launched the Alphafly 4, the newest version of its marathon racing shoe, with changes to nearly every major part. The company says it returns 10% more energy than its predecessor and weighs 5% less in a men's size 8.5.The biggest change is in the midsole. Nike has added a new ZoomX LT foam, which it says is up to 17% lighter than standard ZoomX and offers 8% more energy return. The shoe goes on early, limited sale on nike.com from today, September 17, with wider availability on nike.com and at select stores from October 29.ZoomX LT doesn't fully replace regular ZoomX. Nike layers the two foams above and below the carbon-fibre Flyplate, which keeps the Alphafly's signature propulsive scoop. The plate adds stability and guides a smooth forward roll, which should help runners hold a steady cadence. Up front, dual Air Zoom units have been retuned to work alongside the foam and plate at push-off. A lightweight Fast Shot outsole handles grip.The new Atomknit upper is seamless and breathable. It uses zoned midfoot cables, an integrated heel unit and a molded sock liner to hold the foot securely over long distances.Nike says development drew on athlete feedback across Alphafly generations, learnings from Project Dreamweaver, and extensive women's trials. Emily Farina, Senior Principal, Running Footwear, Nike Sport Research Lab, said the team studied how fatigue changes running mechanics."Our goal was simple: create a shoe that helps athletes feel more confident and capable deep into the race," she said.Nike athlete Addisu Gobena has already tested that claim. He wore the Alphafly 4 to a course-record marathon win in Sydney, and said he trusted the shoe when the race got difficult.
Article Summary: Nike alphafly 4 is the newest version of its marathon racing shoe. The company says it returns 10% more energy than its predecessor and weighs 5% less in a men's size 8.5. Nike has added a new zoomx lt foam, which it says is up to 17% lighter than standard zoomx.
